summary.text: Gwen Moore is the Democratic incumbent representing Wisconsin's 4th District (Milwaukee) since 2005, the first African American elected to Congress from Wisconsin. Before Congress she was a VISTA volunteer, a housing and social services official, and a state legislator for 15 years. She serves on the House Ways and Means Committee and the Joint Economic Committee and is seeking another term.

paragraphs.text: Moore was born in Racine, Wisconsin, in 1951 and raised in Milwaukee, the eighth of nine children; her father was a union factory worker and her mother a public school teacher.
She attended North Division High School in Milwaukee, where she was student council president.

She earned a bachelor's degree in political science from Marquette University, which she says she attended as a single, expectant mother with help from the federal TRIO program, and later received a Harvard University Certificate for Senior Executives in State and Local Government in 2000.
Sources differ on the year of her Marquette degree.

Moore began her career as a VISTA volunteer, helping to start a community credit union and receiving the national "VISTA Volunteer of the Decade" award for 1976-1986, according to her official biography.

She then worked as a housing officer for the Wisconsin Housing Development Authority; WUWM, drawing on her campaign website, says she worked for the City of Milwaukee and the state on housing and social services issues.
Moore served two terms in the Wisconsin State Assembly (1989-1992) and then in the Wisconsin State Senate from 1993 to 2004.
She was elected to the U.S. House in 2004, defeating Republican attorney Gerald Boyle with 69.6% of the vote according to Wikipedia, and took office on January 3, 2005.

In the House, Moore serves on the Ways and Means Committee (Tax, Social Security, and Work and Welfare subcommittees) and the Joint Economic Committee, and co-chairs the bipartisan Congressional Caucus on Foster Youth.
She previously served on the Financial Services, Science, Space, and Technology, and Budget committees, and was Democratic co-chair of the Congressional Women's Caucus from 2011 to 2013.
She is a member of the Congressional Black Caucus and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, among others.
WUWM describes her as the longest-serving current member of Wisconsin's U.S. House delegation, and she won the August 11, 2026 Democratic primary over Amy Donahue, 70.5% to 29.3%.
According to her official biography, she is the mother of three and a grandmother and great-grandmother.
